name: Pregabalin + Methylcobalamin + Nortriptyline
meta: Pregabalin 75 mg + Methylcobalamin 500/1500 mcg + Nortriptyline 10 mg

Pregabalin: Gabapentinoid (neuropathic pain / anxiolytic / antiepileptic); Methylcobalamin: Active vitamin B12 coenzyme (neurotrophic); Nortriptyline Hydrochloride: Tricyclic antidepressant (secondary amine)
Pregabalin: N02BF02 (previously N03AX16); Methylcobalamin: B03BA05; Nortriptyline Hydrochloride: N06AA10
Prescription-only fixed-dose combination. Components – Pregabalin: Schedule H –
prescription only; Methylcobalamin: Prescription combination ingredient; Nortriptyline Hydrochloride: Schedule H – prescription only
sections: White to off-white crystalline solid, freely soluble in water.
Cobalamin (corrinoid) – methyl coenzyme form of vitamin B12
Bright red crystals or crystalline powder; light-sensitive.
White to off-white powder (hydrochloride), soluble in water.

Pregabalin: Developed as a more potent successor to gabapentin; pain relief may begin within the first week. First approval/introduction: Synthesised 1990 (Richard B. Silverman, Northwestern University); EU and US FDA 2004 (Pfizer). Methylcobalamin: One of the two active coenzyme forms of vitamin B12 (with adenosylcobalamin), used widely in India and Japan for peripheral neuropathy. First approval/introduction: Mecobalamin approved in Japan (Eisai) for peripheral neuropathy. Nortriptyline Hydrochloride: The N-desmethyl active metabolite of amitriptyline; first described and patented in 1962. First approval/introduction: Introduced 1963; US approval 1964 (Geigy).
Pregabalin 75 mg + Methylcobalamin 500/1500 mcg + Nortriptyline 10 mg
Triple approach – pregabalin and nortriptyline relieve pain by distinct mechanisms while methylcobalamin supports nerve regeneration.

Pregabalin Binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels with higher affinity than gabapentin, decreasing release of excitatory neurotransmitters; analgesic, anxiolytic and anticonvulsant. Receptor / target profile: Binds the alpha-2-delta-1 protein of voltage-gated calcium channels with high affinity, reducing release of glutamate, norepinephrine and substance P.

Methylcobalamin Coenzyme for methionine synthase; promotes myelin and nucleic-acid synthesis, axonal regeneration and remyelination of damaged peripheral nerves; reduces homocysteine. Receptor / target profile: Cofactor for methionine synthase; promotes myelin and axonal protein synthesis.

Nortriptyline Hydrochloride Predominantly inhibits norepinephrine reuptake (and serotonin to a lesser extent); enhances descending noradrenergic pain inhibition. Fewer anticholinergic and sedative effects than amitriptyline.
Receptor / target profile: Potent NET inhibitor (Ki 1.8–4.4 nM) and moderate SERT inhibitor (Ki 15–18 nM); weaker H1 and muscarinic antagonism than amitriptyline.
Summary: Bioavailability ≥90% (linear); Tmax ~1 h. Not protein bound; negligible metabolism. Half-life ~6.3 h. Renally excreted unchanged – adjust dose to CrCl.
Oral ~1–2% by passive diffusion at high doses; intrinsic-factor-mediated absorption
Summary: Absorbed via intrinsic factor and passive diffusion; stored in liver; excreted in urine and bile.
Summary: Well absorbed; Tmax 7–8.5 h. ~92% protein bound. Metabolised by CYP2D6. Half-life 18–44 h.

Pregabalin: Renal function; weight; oedema; misuse; respiratory status.
Nortriptyline Hydrochloride: Plasma levels (therapeutic window 50–150 ng/mL for depression); ECG in cardiac disease.

Pregabalin: Somnolence, confusion, agitation, restlessness, seizures (rare), coma. Supportive care; haemodialysis effective. Methylcobalamin: Very low toxicity. Nortriptyline Hydrochloride: As for TCAs – arrhythmias, seizures, coma. ECG monitoring and supportive care.
Evidence derives from component trials; no large randomised trials of the triple combination.
Dizziness, drowsiness and weight gain may occur
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
